title: Bacterial concrete: the future of self-healing and sustainable infrastructure
author: Sukumaran, Johnpaul, et al.

steps.title: Select and Prepare Raw Materials
steps.instruction: Gather Ordinary Portland Cement (OPC) grade 33 (IS 12269:2013) as the binder; obtain fine aggregate (river sand, Zone II, specific gravity 2.65, fineness modulus 2.8) and coarse aggregate (crushed granite, 20 mm size, specific gravity 2.7) complying with IS 383:2016; use clean potable water for mixing and curing; include fly ash (244 kg m⁻³) where required by the mix design.

substeps.instruction: Measure fine aggregate specific gravity (2.65) and fineness modulus (2.8).
Measure coarse aggregate size (20 mm) and specific gravity (2.7).
Verify water is free of impurities.
Prepare fly ash if the mix calls for it.

steps.title: Prepare Bacterial Suspensions
steps.instruction: Cultivate the five bacterial strains—Bacillus subtilis, Bacillus licheniformis, Bacillus flexus, Pseudomonas stutzeri, and Escherichia coli—and adjust each culture to the required cell concentration of 10⁴, 10⁵, or 10⁶ cells ml⁻¹ as indicated for each concrete mix.

substeps.instruction: Grow each strain under appropriate conditions.
Harvest cells and resuspend in sterile water.
Count cells and dilute or concentrate to reach 10⁴, 10⁵, or 10⁶ cells ml⁻¹.

steps.title: Formulate Concrete Mixes
steps.instruction: For each mix designation (M1–M16) weigh cement 399 kg m⁻³, fly ash 244 kg m⁻³ (if specified), fine aggregate 44.87 kg m⁻³, coarse aggregate 100 kg m⁻³, and water 40 kg m⁻³; add the bacterial suspension at the concentration shown in Table 1 (‑‑ for no bacteria, 10⁴, 10⁵, or 10⁶ cells ml⁻¹); mix thoroughly to obtain a homogeneous concrete matrix.

substeps.instruction: Weigh cement, fly ash, fine aggregate, coarse aggregate, and water according to the table.
Introduce the bacterial suspension at the prescribed concentration.
Mix using a mechanical mixer until uniform consistency is achieved.

steps.title: Cast Specimens
steps.instruction: Pour the fresh concrete into the three types of molds: cubes 15 × 15 × 15 cm for compressive strength, cylinders 15 cm diameter × 30 cm height for splitting tensile strength, and beams 15 × 15 × 750 cm for flexural strength; place concrete in successive layers, compact each layer with tamping rods or vibration, level the top surface, and cover the molds for 24 h to prevent moisture loss.

substeps.instruction: Compact each layer to remove air voids.
Level the surface after the final layer.
Cover molds and keep them undisturbed for 24 hours.

steps.title: Demold and Water‑Cure
steps.instruction: After the 24‑hour covering period, demold the specimens and immerse them in clean water for curing until the scheduled testing age of 7 days or 28 days.

substeps.instruction: Place specimens in a water tank with continuous water supply.
Maintain curing until the desired testing age (7 d or 28 d).

description: The effectiveness of bacterial concrete is significantly influenced by the characteristics of the materials incorporated into its formulation, as each element is vital in establishing its mechanical strength, longevity, and ability to withstand environmental deterioration. Ordinary Portland Cement (OPC) of 33-grade, compliant with IS 12269:2013, was utilized as the main binding agent. The selection of OPC 33-grade is attributed to its superior early strength, which facilitates improved hydration and enhances the performance of bacterial concrete [37]. The chemical makeup of the cement, particularly the presence of tricalcium silicate (C3S) and dicalcium silicate (C2S), is vital for the hydration process, thereby affecting the overall strength development and durability of the concrete matrix. Fine aggregate, sourced from locally available river sand (Zone II) in accordance with IS 383:2016, was utilized to achieve optimal gradation and workability. This fine aggregate exhibited a specific gravity of 2.65 and a fineness modulus of 2.8, demonstrating its appropriateness for the production of dense and workable concrete. The fine aggregate plays a crucial role by occupying the voids between cement particles, thereby minimizing porosity and enhancing the overall compactness of the concrete. Coarse aggregate, composed of crushed granite with a size of 20 mm, was employed to facilitate improved interlocking and load distribution [38]. The choice of crushed granite, recognized for its exceptional hardness and durability, contributes to the enhancement of both compressive and flexural strength of the concrete. The specific gravity of the coarse aggregate was recorded at 2.7, and it adhered to the standards set forth in IS 383:2016 to ensure uniformity in the mix. Clean, potable water devoid of impurities was utilized for both mixing and curing, in accordance with the standards set forth in IS 456:2000.
